title: Particles and States of Matter
seo_title: Grade 6 States of Matter Worksheets: Particle Motion, Changes of State and Heating Curves
standard_text: Develop a model that predicts and describes changes in particle motion, temperature, and state of a pure substance when thermal energy is added or removed.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on particles and states of matter (NGSS MS-PS1-4): particle diagrams of solids, liquids and gases, melting, boiling and condensation, and heating curve data. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Thermal energy changes how fast particles move.
key_sub: Adding energy speeds particles up and can melt or boil a substance. Removing energy slows them and can condense or freeze it.
body_html:
How to think about it

All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. Adding thermal energy makes them move faster; removing it makes them move slower.

When particles move fast enough, the state can change: melting and boiling/evaporation need energy added; freezing and condensation need energy removed. During a change of state the temperature stays the same: water stays at 0 °C while it melts and at 100 °C while it boils.

Example

Water vapor forms drops on a cold can. Energy added or removed?

Gas → liquid is condensation.

Answer: removed

Example

What happens to particles when ice melts?

Energy is added.

Particles move faster and slide past each other.

Answer: They move faster and are no longer fixed in place.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking particles in a solid do not move.
  • Thinking particles get bigger when heated.
  • Thinking temperature keeps rising while water boils.

faq.q: How do particles move in solids, liquids and gases?
faq.a: In solids they vibrate in place, in liquids they slide past each other, and in gases they move fast and far apart.

faq.q: What happens to particles when a substance is heated?
faq.a: They move faster and spread out. The particles themselves do not get bigger.

faq.q: Why does temperature stay the same while water boils?
faq.a: The added energy is used to change liquid water into gas, not to raise the temperature.

items.q: Which diagram shows chocolate in the state where it has particles close together but able to slide past each other?
items.e: That is a liquid.

items.q: Ethan observes butter in a hot pan. What happens to the motion of the particles?
items.e: Adding energy speeds particles up; removing energy slows them down.

items.q: These diagrams show particles of butter. Which diagram shows the solid state?
items.e: A solid has particles packed tightly and vibrating in place.

items.q: What does temperature measure?
c: the average motion (energy) of the particles
items.e: Higher temperature means faster particles.

items.q: Do the particles in a solid move?
items.e: Particles are always moving.

items.q: Which diagram shows aluminum in the state where it has particles packed tightly and vibrating in place?
items.e: That is a solid.

items.q: In which state are particles farthest apart?
c: They are the same in all states.
items.e: Gas particles spread out to fill their container.

items.q: Ava observes water bubbling in a pot on the stove. What change of state is this?
items.e: Boiling: liquid → gas, with thermal energy added.

items.q: Why can a liquid be poured?
c: Its particles are locked in place.
Its particles can slide past each other.
items.e: Liquids flow but keep the same volume.

items.q: When water vapor touches a cold window and forms drops, what happens to the particles?
c: They lose energy, slow down and come closer together.
items.e: Condensation removes thermal energy.
